root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/commands.rs. Top-level dispatch correctly special-cases apply: dispatch_analyser_hook (~line 592-636) routes Hook::Apply to handle_apply_command (defined in rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/handlers.rs:909), whose doc comment (handlers.rs:883-908) explicitly states its job is to stop the generic ArgRole::Body recursion from misreading the lambda's parameter list as a command. But nested/substitution-context commands go through a separate path: run_nested_command_diagnostics (commands.rs:1515) -> collect_substitution_segments/collect_segment_recursive (commands.rs:2591-2643) -> dispatch_nested_segment (commands.rs:1651). collect_segment_recursive's generic ArgRole::Body descent (line 2631-2641) is gated only by `!definition_handler_owns_body(registry, seg.name())` (line 2632), which checks CommandSpec.definition_body — true for proc/class-definers but NOT set for apply (apply is wired via analyser_hook, not definition_body — see rust/tcl-registry/src/commands/tcl/apply.rs:56). So apply's Body-role argument (the whole lambda literal) falls through to the generic descend_command/segments_from_tree script-walk, which — exactly as the handlers.rs comment predicts — treats "{params} {body}" as one script command with cmd_name = the dequoted params-list text. Separately, dispatch_nested_segment (commands.rs:1651-1780) explicitly re-special-cases Hook::Proc and Hook::OoDefine for nested segments (lines 1763-1780) but has no arm for Hook::Apply, so even that secondary guard doesn't catch it. Fix would be to either add `apply` to definition_handler_owns_body's exclusion set (or an analogous Apply-aware check) in collect_segment_recursive, and/or add a Hook::Apply arm in dispatch_nested_segment that calls the equivalent of handle_apply_command for nested-substitution call sites.

summary: The analyser's I230 "constant [info exists X]" fold in rust/tcl-compiler/src/sccp.rs::existence_constant_branches() falsely reports a reachable branch as unreachable when a variable is only ever set indirectly via `set $var value` (the exact argparse.tcl:100-108 idiom: `set $switch {}` where $switch's value comes from a static, enumerable tcl::prefix-match candidate list). Because `set` with a non-literal (substituted) LHS name lowers to a generic Call with an empty `defs` list (lowering/mod.rs::set_literal_body bails when the name token contains '$'), the variable never enters existence_constant_branches' `defined` set, so `[info exists mixed]` (etc.) is folded to a constant `false` and the analyser emits an I230 diagnostic claiming the true-branch of a genuinely reachable `if` is dead code — even though tclsh proves the branch executes.

root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-compiler/src/sccp.rs, fn existence_constant_branches() (~line 851): the `defined` set is built only from Statement::AssignConst/AssignExpr/AssignValue/Incr `name` fields and Statement::Call `defs`. A `set $var value` (dynamic/substituted LHS) lowers via rust/tcl-compiler/src/lowering/mod.rs::set_literal_body() — which correctly declines when the name token contains '$' (line ~312) — down to a generic Statement::Call with an empty defs list, so it contributes nothing to `defined` and isn't treated as an escape hatch either (unlike the `aliased`/scan_scope_aliases skip-list already added for `namespace upvar`, per the FP-RBS-05 fix, or the whole-function Statement::Barrier bail at the top of the same function). Fix direction: treat a `set`/`array set`/`lappend`/etc. Call whose first argument is a non-literal (substitution-containing) variable-name as either (a) adding to a new "dynamically-written, existence-unknown" set that existence_constant_branches consults before folding any `[info exists X]` for `X` in scope, or (b) reusing the existing whole-function Barrier bail-out, mirroring the treatment already given to `namespace upvar`. Related/relevant existing tests: rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/fp/rbs.rs fp_rbs_05_alias_exists_guard_is_not_constant (the analogous namespace-upvar fix), and rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/state.rs w216_brace_then_paren_name_vs_value_positions (documents that bare `set $x v` is deliberately still flagged by W212 as "the dynamic-name foot-gun" — i.e., the codebase already recognizes this exact construct as a distinct, real pattern, just hasn't wired it into the existence-fold's defined-set/escape-hatch logic).

root_cause_hint:
rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/dataflow.rs::emit_unused_variable_diagnostics (~line 538) flags a var as unused when no SSA def-use chain for it is live. Liveness comes from rust/tcl-compiler/src/ssa.rs::uses_of() (~line 1108-1192): for Statement::Barrier (which `info locals` lowers to) it only calls scan_command_words() over the barrier's own literal tokens — it has no notion that a frame-inspecting `info locals`/`info vars` enumeration followed by any dynamic per-name dereference should be treated as reading every local in scope.

The codebase already has exactly this concept, but in a sibling module that the diagnostics pipeline does not consult: rust/tcl-compiler/src/var_escape/info_subcommands.rs defines FRAME_INSPECTING_SUBCOMMANDS (includes "locals", "vars", "level", "frame", "coroutine", "errorstack") and rust/tcl-compiler/src/var_escape/cfg_propagation/handlers.rs::handle_info (~line 149-170) forces a pessimistic "escape everything" fallback whenever one of these fires. That var_escape module is wired only into inlining/var_scoping (rust/tcl-compiler/src/inlining/, rust/tcl-compiler/src/var_scoping.rs) for codegen slot-allocation correctness — grep confirms analyser/diagnostics never references var_escape. The fix is to either route the diagnostics dataflow builder through the same is_frame_inspecting_info_subcommand() check (suppressing W211 for all locals in a unit that contains a frame-inspecting `info` call), or add an equivalent barrier-escapes-all-locals rule directly in ssa.rs's uses_of()/Statement::Barrier arm.
failure_scenario: A proc that does `foreach locVar [info locals] { ... dict append out $locVar [subst $[subst $locVar]] ... }` (verbatim pattern from georgtree_argparse's test/arbitaryTest.tcl:15-21, used to auto-serialize every argparse-produced local into a result dict) has each of its plain `set`-created locals (e.g. `set alpha 10`) flagged with a HINT: "Variable 'alpha' is set but never used" — even though tclsh execution proves alpha's value of 10 is read and appears in the returned dict. A developer trusting this hint and deleting the "unused" `set alpha 10` line would silently break the running program (the dict would lose the `alpha` entry, or in the real argparse-derived case, an argparse switch's captured value would vanish from the result).

summary: In argparse.tcl:380-382 the proc-body-local, conditionally-gated `namespace import textutil::adjust::*` is actually tracked fine by the analyser (verified with a control repro of a user-defined namespace: hover/go-to-def both correctly resolve bare `foo`/`bar` after the same in-body conditional-import pattern). summary: Cross-document find-references (and by extension rename-safety) silently misses call sites that live in a `.test` file, because the LSP's background workspace scan hard-codes an allowed-extension list that omits `.test` — the standard tcltest extension used throughout the real corpus (test/argparse.test, sourced exactly this way from test/all_codeCoverage.tcl).
failure_scenario:
Root cause confirmed at rust/tcl-lsp-server/src/lib.rs:11985-12002, `fn is_tcl_source(path)`: `matches!(path.extension()..., Some("tcl"|"tk"|"itcl"|"tm"|"irul"|"irule"|"iapp"|"iappimpl"|"impl"|"exp"|"apl"))` — `.test` is not in the list. 2) W113 false positive (CONFIRMED). Real corpus file copied verbatim to audit/11/real/argparse.tcl. Oracle: `echo 'puts [info commands argparse]; puts [catch {argparse} e]; puts $e' | tclsh9.0` (and tclsh8.6) → empty command list, then `invalid command name "argparse"` — proving `argparse` is NOT a Tcl 8.6/9.0 built-in before the package defines it. Reproduced identically and deterministically on a second run, and also reproduced in the minimal analog (argparse_mini.tcl:21, same message). This is a false diagnostic on a statically-resolvable question: the registry's own `CommandSpec` for `argparse` already carries `required_package: Some("argparse")` (rust/tcl-registry/src/commands/argparse/command.rs:252) — the exact field the neighbouring W120 "requires package require" check (rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/unresolved.rs, ~line 615: `if spec.required_package.is_none() { continue; }`) already uses to know `argparse` is package-gated, not core — but `Analyser::builtin_command_names()` (rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/state.rs:1537-1549) unions it into the same "built-in" set as genuine core Tcl commands (`registry.command_names()` over tcl+stdlib+tcllib+argparse+ticklecharts+itcl+tk+irules+...), and `Analyser::emit_w113_proc_shadows_builtin()` (rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/handlers.rs:526-566) only excludes namespace-qualified names and `overridable_library_procs()` (core script-defined library procs like `unknown`/`auto_*`) — never `required_package`. So any proc/command literally named after a registered third-party package command (argparse, or any tcllib/itcl/ticklecharts/eda_* command) gets a false "shadows built-in" warning even when the real Tcl built-in set has no such command at all.
root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/state.rs:1537-1549 (`builtin_command_names`, pulls `registry.command_names()` — the full package-inclusive command universe — into the W113 "built-in" set) feeding rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/handlers.rs:526-566 (`emit_w113_proc_shadows_builtin`, filters only on namespace-qualification + `overridable_library_procs()`, never on `CommandSpec::required_package`). Contrast with rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/unresolved.rs (`emit_missing_package_require_diagnostics`, ~line 615) which already reads `spec.required_package` correctly for the opposite purpose. Fix: exclude any command whose resolved `CommandSpec` has `required_package.is_some()` (or its `tcllib_package` alias, spec.rs:1059) from the W113 shadow-candidate set, the same way namespace-qualified names are already excluded — unless the profile marks that package `is_ambient_package` (as f5-irules' `pool` correctly still is).

summary: Hover and find-references silently return nothing for a class member whose *own* declaration lives in a class-reopening `oo::define ClassName { ... }` block appended after the class's `oo::class create`/`oo::configurable create` block — exactly the shape of src/generalClasses.tcl:365-374, where `method <WriteProp-value>` is defined in a second `oo::define Parameter { ... }` block. - `hover repro.tcl 24 15` (cursor on the <WriteProp-value> token at its own `method` declaration, line 25 1-based) → `(no hover)`, swept every column 11-28 across the whole token, all empty.

Same file, same harness, same cursor mechanics — only the block the method lives in differs.

To rule out the confound that `<WriteProp-value>`'s odd bracketed name (not plain alphanumerics) is what breaks it (a separate, real bug — see below), isolate3.tcl uses a PLAIN identifier method name defined purely in a reopening block: `oo::class create Foo { method plain {} {...} }` then `oo::define Foo { method reopened {val} {...} }`. Same result: `hover isolate3.tcl 6 13` (on `reopened`'s own declaration) → `(no hover)`; `references isolate3.tcl 6 13` → `References (0 locations)`. Yet `definition isolate3.tcl 15 12` (go-to-def FROM the call site `$f reopened hi`) correctly resolves to `isolate3.tcl 6:11-6:19`, and `hover` from that same call site correctly shows `**method** `::Foo::reopened` (1 param(s))`. Control `plain` (first block) hovers/references fine from both directions. This isolates the bug to "cursor is physically inside a reopening oo::define block" rather than to the exotic method name.

Root cause (read from source): `rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/handlers.rs::handle_oo_class_command` sets `ClassDef.body_span` once from the *first* `oo::class create`/`oo::configurable create` body token (~line 2622/2628). `handle_oo_define_command`'s body-form branch (lines 2755-2768) looks up that SAME `ClassDef` via `all_classes.remove(&qualified)` when a later `oo::define ClassName { ... }` reopens the class, and calls `parse_oo_definition_body` (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/oo.rs`) to merge the new block's methods/properties into `class_def.methods`/`.properties` — but that function never updates `class_def.body_span` to also cover the reopening block's span (`ClassDef.body_span` in `rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/types.rs:515` is a single `Span`, not a list). Both `rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/hover.rs::class_member_hover_text` (~line 2718-2726: `body.start() < cursor_offset && cursor_offset < body.end()`) and `rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/definition.rs::lookup_class_member` (~line 306-316, same gate) require the cursor to fall inside `body_span` before consulting `class_def.methods`/`.properties`, so a cursor inside the second block never matches even though the member is present in the map. Call-site dispatch (`instance_method_definition` → `method_dispatch_definition`) doesn't gate on `body_span` at all, which is why it still works — the inconsistency between the two code paths is the tell.

Secondary, compounding bug found in the same investigation: `rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/definition.rs::instance_method_at_cursor`'s `is_ident` closure (line 631: `c.is_alphanumeric() || c == '_' || c == ':'`) excludes `-`, `<`, `>` from method-name characters when parsing a `$obj method` call-site token, so hover/go-to-definition FROM a call site also fails for hyphenated or angle-bracketed method names specifically (independent of the reopening-block issue) — confirmed with a plain, non-reopened `oo::class create Foo { method write-value {...}; method <bracketed> {...} }` (isolate.tcl/isolate2.tcl): `definition isolate2.tcl 12 10` (on the `plain` call, control) → resolves; same test on `write-value`/`<bracketed>` calls → 0 locations at every swept column, while `references` on the same tokens (a different code path) correctly finds both. Non-bug (correctly abstains): hovering/go-to-def on `my configure -value ...` / `$w configure -value ...` (the actual invocation form used throughout the real corpus) returns nothing — this is correct abstention, since resolving TIP-558's implicit property→`<WriteProp-NAME>` wiring is a deep runtime-configure-machinery inference the LSP doesn't attempt; not counted as a bug here.

root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-lsp-server/src/lib.rs `compute_definition` (~line 3633-3706): after the in-document `core_definition::definition` call comes back empty, the function gates the cross-file fallback with `if !on_command_head { return Ok(Vec::new()); }` (line ~3689), where `on_command_head` comes from `position_is_command_head` (~line 10074-10082), which only tests whether the cursor falls inside `analysis.command_invocations` — i.e. a command's own head token. Even if it were reached, `resolve_workspace_symbols`'s own doc-comment (~line 3952-3954) states it deliberately resolves "a bareword argument" to nothing, so that function would need updating too. summary: find-references is completely blind to `interp alias {} NAME {} TARGET` (matches the real pattern's `interp alias {} @ {} lindex` / `{} = {} expr`, `test/codeCoverage.tcl:17-22`). Go-to-definition and hover DO resolve the alias correctly (hover shows "Alias → lindex"/"Alias → expr", and for an alias to a user proc, definition correctly jumps through the alias to the proc), so the punctuation-lexing theory in the note is refuted — `@`/`=` are tokenized and resolved fine. The real, confirmed bug is narrower but real: references.rs never consults `analysis.command_aliases` at all, in either direction. Querying references on the alias name itself returns 0 hits (even though it has real call sites), and — more seriously — querying references on the ALIASED TARGET proc misses every call site reached only through the alias, i.e. `interp alias {} sayHi {} greet` + two `[sayHi]` calls: find-references on `greet`'s declaration returns only the proc decl and the literal "greet" word inside the `interp alias` line itself, silently omitting both real runtime call sites of `greet` (confirmed live via tclsh: `greet`'s body executes twice, printing "hi" twice). Anyone using find-references to gauge whether `greet` (or, in the real project, `lindex`/`expr`-aliased helpers) is safe to remove/rename would be told it has 0 live callers when it actually has 2.

root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/references.rs: the `references()` dispatch chain (variable_references → class_references → proc_references → instance_method_references → class_member_references, lines ~221-269) never consults `analysis.command_aliases`. Contrast rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/definition.rs, which has an explicit alias branch (`lookup_alias(analysis, &word)` at line ~223, backed by `analysis.command_aliases` populated via rust/tcl-compiler/src/alias.rs::detect_interp_alias and rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/handlers.rs::handle_interp_alias/record_interp_alias) that correctly walks alias→target for go-to-definition and (per hover output) for hover too. `proc_references` (references.rs line 389) only calls `resolve_proc_target_at`/`proc_reference_spans`, which match direct literal calls to the proc's own name — they have no path back through `command_aliases` to attribute an alias's call sites to the aliased target, nor any path forward to list an alias name's own call sites. Fix would add a references.rs analogue of definition.rs's `lookup_alias` in both directions: (1) when the cursor word is itself a recorded alias, resolve to the target proc and reuse `proc_reference_spans` for it; (2) when computing references for a target proc, also union in every call site of any alias whose target resolves to that proc.

summary: Go-to-definition/hover/find-references never resolve a variable that a callee creates in the *caller's* frame via `upvar 1 literalOther literalMy` — even for a fully static, single-hop, non-dynamic case. This exactly matches SpiceGenTcl's `Utility::NameProcess` (generalClasses.tcl:117-125, `upvar name name`), mixed into every Dc/Ac/Tran/pulse/sin/... constructor, which is called as `my NameProcess $arguments [self object]` and afterward the constructor reads `$name` (e.g. specAnalysesClassesCommon.tcl:52 then :57 `next dc $params -name $name`) without ever `set`/`variable`-declaring `name` itself.

Isolated the OO indirection away with a minimal non-OO control at .../audit/22/control4/local_only.tcl: `proc setter {} { upvar 1 outerVar innerAlias; set innerAlias hello; puts $innerAlias }` / `proc caller {} { setter; puts $outerVar }`. `tclsh9.0 local_only.tcl` prints `hello` twice (proving `$outerVar` is real in `caller`'s frame). Inside `setter` itself, hover/definition on `$innerAlias` work correctly (hover → "Variable innerAlias, 2 reference(s)"; definition → points at the `upvar` line), confirming intra-proc upvar handling is fine. But in `caller`, hover/definition/references on `$outerVar` (line 8, cols 9-13, i.e. every column of the token) all return empty/`(no hover)` — the exact same class of miss as the OO case, with zero namespace/mixin machinery involved, so it isn't a mixin-resolution problem, it's that caller-side upvar effects are never propagated into the caller's scope at all.
Root cause: `handle_upvar_command` in rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/handlers.rs (~lines 2019-2038) calls `self.define_var(&args[i], ..., scope_path, ...)` using the *callee's own* `scope_path` — i.e. it only registers the `myVar` alias inside the proc/method that contains the `upvar` statement. Nothing in rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/commands.rs's call-handling walks a call site (`proc` call or `my <method>` OO dispatch through `oo_my.rs`) to inspect the resolved callee body for a static (non-dynamic, explicit-level) `upvar` effect and mirror the target variable into the *caller's* scope. This is a one-hop, fully literal, non-dynamic pattern (no computed level, no computed varname, single direct call) — well within "hard but not undecidable" per the audit brief — yet it produces a blank abstention rather than resolving to the defining `upvar` statement.
root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/handlers.rs::handle_upvar_command (~2019-2038) only defines the myVar alias in the callee's own scope_path via Analyser::define_var (rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/scope.rs:746); there is no interprocedural step in rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/commands.rs (plain proc calls) or rust/tcl-registry/src/commands/tcl/oo_my.rs (`my <method>` OO dispatch) that, given a literal call target, looks at the callee's body for a static `upvar 1 literalOther literalMy` and injects `literalOther` as a defined variable in the caller's scope for hover/definition/find-references purposes.

summary: On the literal assigned repro (stdout2var's `eval [subst -nocommands {proc ::puts {args} {...}}]`), the LSP's hover/go-to-def answers for $var/$level (real, subst-substituted refs to stdout2var's own scope) and \$args/\$fd/\$message (backslash-escaped, correctly abstained) all match tclsh ground truth. But this is coincidental, not a real simulation of subst's escaping rules: the shared word-at-cursor resolver (find_var_at_position, rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/hover.rs) does a raw per-line text scan for `$identifier` with zero awareness of comment/string/brace-quoting context. Built a minimal oracle-verified variant (control_inert_brace.tcl) proving it: hover/go-to-definition on a `$level`/`$var`-shaped substring sitting inside a genuinely inert Tcl comment, or inside a plain (non-subst) brace-quoted string literal that tclsh emits byte-for-byte unsubstituted, still confidently resolve as "Variable `level`"/"Variable `var`" and jump to an unrelated declaration -- contradicting the LSP's own semantic-tokens classification (marks the whole comment/string as one opaque token, no nested Var sub-tokens) and its own W220 "assignment is never read" diagnostic (correctly treats those same vars as unused). Root cause confirmed via source read: find_var_at_position is a pure delimiter-based char scan with no CST/token lookup, imported directly by definition.rs and transitively driving references. A closely related, independently-confirmed second bug surfaced in the same investigation: the exact real-world call sequence (stdout2var output; $parser buildTopNetlist; restorestdout; return $output, verbatim from netlistParserClassNgpice.test) makes the LSP emit a false W210 "Variable 'output' is read before it is set" even though tclsh proves output is genuinely set (via the generated proc's uplevel-based indirect assignment). A control using the equivalent upvar-based idiom is correctly suppressed (0 diagnostics), showing the FP-suppression logic (rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/fp/rbs.rs) models upvar aliasing but has no equivalent for uplevel N set $var value, even in plain code with no eval/subst at all -- so this second bug's root cause is broader than the eval/subst mechanic, though it fires squarely on the audited real-world pattern.

root_cause_hint: Primary bug: rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/hover.rs, fn find_var_at_position (~line 2137) -- scans line_text char-by-char for a `$identifier` pattern using only delimiter characters (space/tab/newline/;/{/}/[/]/"/$), never consulting the CST/semantic-token classification for whether the cursor position falls inside a Comment or a non-substituting Str/brace token. Called first-and-unconditionally at the top of hover_with_profile (hover.rs ~line 177) and imported directly into rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/definition.rs (line 82: `use crate::hover::{find_var_at_position, ...}`; used at line 132 inside `definition()`), so go-to-definition inherits the same blindness; references appears to reuse the same "what symbol is under the cursor" step. Contrast with the codebase's own correct handling elsewhere: semantic-tokens (verified via the semantic-tokens subcommand) and the W220 dead-store diagnostic (rust/tcl-compiler analyser) both correctly treat comment/brace-string content as opaque. Secondary bug: rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/fp/rbs.rs -- has explicit, tested false-positive suppression for `upvar`-based indirect writes (e.g. fp_rbs_08_dynamic_upvar_target_silent, fp_rbs_callbyname_upvar_alias_still_suppresses at line ~1547) but no equivalent recognition of `uplevel N [list set $var value]` / `uplevel N set $var value` as a caller-scope definition mechanism, so rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/dataflow.rs's W210 check (message format at dataflow.rs ~line 1125/1355/1542) fires a false positive whenever a variable is set only via that idiom, whether or not it is wrapped in eval/subst.

summary: SpiceGenTcl.tcl:24 does `namespace import ::tcl::mathop::*` at global scope in the bootstrap file, then `source`s generalClasses.tcl, where a bareword `+` is called deep inside a TclOO method body (generalClasses.tcl:89 `oo::class create Utility` -> :2090 `method getDataPoints {args}` -> :2356 `foreach line [lrange $header [+ $i 1] end-1]`), with nothing at the use site marking `+` as an imported command. Built a faithful minimal analogue (main.tcl imports mathop then sources lib.tcl, which defines `namespace eval ::Widget { oo::class create Parser { method parseFrom {header start} { ... [+ $start 1] ... } } }`) and confirmed under both tclsh9.0 and tclsh8.6 that the bareword `+` genuinely resolves to `::tcl::mathop::+` at runtime (and, via a negative control with the import removed, that it is NOT resolvable without it - `invalid command name "+"`). Drove the LSP against both the minimal repro and the real corpus file at the real call site (generalClasses.tcl:2355:46, 0-based) and found fully correct behaviour in both: zero diagnostics (no false unknown-command warning), hover correctly identifies `+` as a built-in command with accurate synopsis, and go-to-definition abstains (0 locations) - which is not a miss, since it is byte-for-byte the same abstention the LSP gives for `puts` and every other core Tcl builtin with no Tcl-level source to jump to. Position-sensitivity was double-checked (neighbouring columns for `[`, `lrange`, `$start` all differ correctly) to rule out harness misuse. Root cause of the correct behaviour: rust/tcl-registry/src/commands/tcl/mathop_generated.rs registers bare `+`/`-`/`*`/etc. unconditionally (all three spellings: bare, `tcl::mathop::+`, `::tcl::mathop::+`), so rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/unresolved.rs's `w123_invocation_resolves` short-circuits on `known.registry_names.contains(name)` before any cross-file `namespace_imports` tracking is even needed, and rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/definition.rs's `resolve_called_proc` deliberately returns `None` once `registry.get(word).is_some()` (line ~1131), so `definition()` abstains instead of guessing.

Root cause of the correct behaviour, from a quick read of the Rust source: rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/unresolved.rs `w123_invocation_resolves` (~line 360) treats every command name containing `::` as resolved (conservative skip) regardless of package-require state, and `emit_unresolved_command_diagnostics` (~line 107) gates W123 off file-wide the moment `self.result.package_requires` is non-empty anywhere in the document - the `conditional` flag recorded per-require (signature_scan/handlers.rs `handle_package`) is tracked but W123/W120 never filter on it, so nesting/conditionality can't cause a false unknown-command here; W120 (`emit_missing_package_require_diagnostics`) only fires for registry-known commands with a `required_package` entry, and niche external packages like ngspicetclbridge aren't in the registry so it never applies to them either. summary: Workspace-wide "Find References" (and by the same mechanism go-to-definition-into-the-file / workspace symbols) silently omits call sites that live in `.test`-extension files, because the passive on-disk workspace scan's extension allowlist (`is_tcl_source` in rust/tcl-lsp-server/src/lib.rs) never included "test" — the standard tcltest suite-file extension. SpiceGenTcl's own test/all_codeCoverage.tcl:17-27 reaches all 19 of its real `.test` files (test/*.test, test/{ngspice,ltspice,xyce}/*.test) exclusively via a non-literal `foreach file $testFiles { source $file }` loop over `glob` results, so — unlike a `.tcl` sibling with identical content — none of that project's `.test` suite has any other static path into the index. The dynamic-source/glob part of the pattern is itself handled correctly (the analyser abstains, no false claim); the bug is the separate, purely-static extension gate that this real pattern happens to make unreachable any other way.

root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-lsp-server/src/lib.rs: is_tcl_source() (~L12003-12020) is the extension allowlist (`tcl, tk, itcl, tm, irul, irule, iapp, iappimpl, impl, exp, apl`) that collect_tcl_files() (~L12028) / scan_workspace_folders() (~L6826) use to decide which on-disk files get passively analysed into WorkspaceIndex; "test" is absent, and the omission is locked in by the unit test is_tcl_source_matches_the_full_tcl_family_extension_set (~L17457-17468), which enumerates exactly this (incomplete) set. A `.test` file only enters the index if the editor opens it directly, or a literal/statically-foldable `source` edge reaches it via resolve_source_edge/resolve_source_uri (~L11512-11539, extension-agnostic). Confirmed-correct, unrelated behaviour: handle_source_command (tcl-compiler/src/analyser/handlers.rs ~L2777-2810) marks `source $file` as `is_literal:false` (Var token / `$`), and auto_path_eval::evaluate_auto_path_expr (tcl-compiler/src/auto_path_eval.rs) explicitly refuses any `$`-containing word — so the analyser correctly abstains on the dynamic glob-loop source calls themselves; there is no glob-simulation anywhere (glob's CommandSpec in tcl-registry/src/commands/tcl/glob_.rs carries no analyser_hook). root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-lsp-server/src/lib.rs, fn resolve_workspace_symbols (~lines 3955-3990), specifically line 3974: `analysis.all_procs.values().find(|p| covers(p.name_span))`. `all_procs: HashMap<String, ProcDef>` is declared in rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/types.rs:773 and populated by a plain `self.result.all_procs.insert(qualified.clone(), proc.clone())` in rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/handlers.rs:741-743 for every `proc` statement in source order - so for a qualified name defined twice, only the last-processed ProcDef's name_span survives, and an earlier/shadowed same-name declaration's own token can never satisfy the `covers()` scan. Every cross-file caller of resolve_workspace_symbols inherits the resulting empty-symbol-set: cross_document_references (~4049-4100, feeds the `references` handler at ~8083 and the reference-count code lens at ~4108), add_cross_document_rename_edits (~4593-4624) and add_workspace_resolved_rename_edits (~4634-4668) (both feed `rename` at ~9692), and prepare_rename's consumer-document fallback (~9676-9689). Fix sketch: resolve_workspace_symbols's declaration branch should recognize the cursor is on ANY `proc`/`oo::class` declaration syntactically matching a qualified name (e.g. by deriving the qualified name from the enclosing declaration's AST node at that offset, the way core_definition::definition() already does successfully) rather than only the one ProcDef the all_procs HashMap happens to retain.
failure_scenario: A user opens tclopt.tcl (or the minimal repro's lib.tcl), places the cursor on the FIRST of the two verbatim `proc ::tclopt::List2array` declarations (an entirely plausible thing to do - e.g. scrolling from the top of the file, or specifically because they suspect it's dead code and want to check), and invokes "Find All References" or "Rename Symbol". Find References silently omits any cross-file caller (proven: main.tcl's call vanishes from the result set versus querying the same symbol from its winning declaration or from a call site, which both correctly include it) - a developer trusting the "0 external callers" implication could delete what they believe is now-orphaned code and break a live caller in another file. Rename is worse: invoking rename from that same shadowed declaration and accepting the edit (which VS Code would apply blindly, trusting the server) leaves the cross-file caller referencing the old name; because a second/dead definition with that old name is still lying around in the same file (exactly the corpus's duplicate-proc idiom), the program does not even crash - it silently starts executing the previously-dead, functionally-different proc body for that caller. Demonstrated end-to-end: applying the LSP's own proposed WorkspaceEdit turns `direct-call-result: IARR {10 20 30}` into `direct-call-result: IARR {0 0 0}` with no error surfaced anywhere.

summary: Two distinct questions live in this finding, and the LSP gets them oppositely: (1) resolving what `{*}$funct $xall $pdata` actually calls at runtime is genuinely dynamic (funct's value comes from whichever `-funct` string a caller passed at construction) and the LSP correctly ABSTAINS there (no false claim) -- that part is REFUTED as a bug. (2) resolving `$funct` as a VARIABLE back to its `variable funct ...` declaration is ordinary, 100%-static TclOO lexical scoping, and the LSP gets it CONFIRMED-wrong: go-to-definition/hover/find-references on `$funct` (and on every other name in the same `variable` statement: `m`, `ftol`, `xtol`, `pdata`, `results`, etc.) inside `::tclopt::Mpfit::run` return nothing, because `::tclopt::Mpfit`'s class body has TWO separate `variable` statements (`variable funct m ftol ... histfreq` at tclopt.tcl:611, then a separate `variable Pars` at tclopt.tcl:613) and the analyser's per-statement handler assigns `class_def.variables = sub_args.to_vec()` instead of accumulating, so the second `variable` statement silently overwrites/discards every name from the first. Only `Pars` (the last statement) survives as a recognised instance variable; `funct` and 15 sibling names become invisible to navigation even though they are declared, used, and correctly interpreted by tclsh. This is not specific to Mpfit -- DE, GSA and LBFGS in the same file use the identical two-statement `variable ...` / `variable Pars` idiom, so the same breakage applies to all four real optimiser classes in this package.
failure_scenario: Any TclOO class body (oo::configurable or plain oo::class) with 2+ separate top-level `variable` statements: only the LAST statement's names remain resolvable. Minimal trigger: `oo::configurable create ::opt::Mpfit { variable funct m pdata results; variable Pars; method run {} { {*}$funct $pdata } }`. tclsh proves `funct`/`pdata` are perfectly valid, live instance variables (the constructed object runs `run` and calls the callback correctly). The LSP's go-to-definition on `$funct` inside `run` returns 0 locations (false "not found") while the sibling `$Pars`, declared in the surviving last statement, correctly resolves. Swapping statement order (`variable Pars` first, `variable funct m pdata results` second) exactly flips which name resolves -- proving "last variable statement wins" as the precise mechanism. Reproduced verbatim against the real corpus file: `cd .../real_verify && python3 lsp_client.py definition tclopt.tcl 946 33` (the exact `{*}$funct $xall $pdata` call site, tclopt.tcl:947 1-based) returns 0 locations, and the same for `$m` at tclopt.tcl:935 (`if {$m<$nfree}`), while a plain local `$xall` on the very same line 946/947 resolves fine to its `lappend xall` declaration -- so the file/method analyses correctly in general; only class instance variables declared in a non-last `variable` statement are affected.

root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/workspace_index.rs, `WorkspaceIndex::index_command_links` (fn starts ~line 374): the loop lifting a document's `namespace import` records (`analysis.namespace_imports`) into cross-file `WorkspaceCommandLink { linked_qname -> target_qname }` entries bails out before indexing any glob pattern -- line 380: `if imp.pattern.contains(['*', '?', '[']) { continue; }`, with the comment "A glob pattern names no single command, so it introduces no link." Consumers `command_link_map()` / `follow_links()` / `resolve_command_target()` / `link_target_spans()` (same file, ~lines 1160-1233) are called from rust/tcl-lsp-server/src/lib.rs at ~line 4023 (`index.resolve_command_target(cand)`, inside the cross-file candidate-resolution path that feeds go-to-definition) and ~line 4082 (`index.link_target_spans(...)`, feeding find-references) -- so a bare name that exists in the workspace only via a wildcard import never gets a link entry, and the plain command-resolution-candidate algorithm (rust/tcl-syntax/src/naming.rs `command_resolution_candidates`, which documents current-namespace + `namespace path` + global only, with no mention of `namespace import` at all) has no other way to connect the bare name to its real, differently-qualified target. summary: In tclopt.tcl, `::tclopt::DuplChecker` is `mixin`'d into `::tclopt::Optimization` (line 504), which `Mpfit`/`DE`/`GSA`/`LBFGS` `superclass`. `Optimization::addPars` calls `my duplListCheck` (line 568), reaching `DuplChecker::duplListCheck` (line 256) only via this mixin-then-superclass chain. go-to-definition resolves this correctly (proving it's statically decidable), but find-references and hover at that exact same call-site token both return nothing, while the identical query from the declaration side correctly finds the call site. Root cause: `references.rs`/`hover.rs`'s "$obj method" resolver never special-cases the `my` receiver the way `definition.rs` does, so it looks up `analysis.instance_classes.get("my")` (always None) and bails, and the fallback class-member scan only checks the enclosing class's *own* method map (not mixin/superclass-inherited providers).
failure_scenario: Repro (matches tclopt.tcl:254-272,503-580 structure): oo::configurable create ::tclopt::DuplChecker { self mixin -append oo::abstract; method duplListCheck {list} {...} }; oo::configurable create ::tclopt::Optimization { mixin ::tclopt::DuplChecker; self mixin -append oo::abstract; method addPars {args} { set dup [my duplListCheck $args]; return $dup } }; oo::configurable create ::tclopt::Mpfit { superclass ::tclopt::Optimization }. Real corpus file (unmodified, cwd=real_ws/) at the real line/col (0-based): `definition tclopt.tcl 567 20` -> "Definition (1 locations): tclopt.tcl 255:11-255:24" (CORRECT, points at DuplChecker::duplListCheck). `references tclopt.tcl 567 20` -> "References (0 locations)" (WRONG - misses both the declaration and the call site itself). `references tclopt.tcl 255 11` (same symbol, queried from the declaration) -> "References (2 locations): tclopt.tcl 255:11-255:24, tclopt.tcl 567:20-567:33" (proves the link is known and correctly indexed elsewhere in the system). `hover tclopt.tcl 567 20` -> "(no hover)" (WRONG); contrast `hover tclopt.tcl 565 41` on the sibling call `my getAllParsNames` two lines earlier in the SAME method, which IS directly owned by Optimization -> "**method** `::tclopt::Optimization::getAllParsNames` (1 param(s))" (correct). Reproduced identically on a minimal from-scratch repro and confirmed non-mixin-specific: a plain `superclass`-only inherited method (`oo::class create A {method foo{x}{...}}; oo::class create B {superclass A; method bar{y}{return [my foo $y]}}`) shows the exact same asymmetry (definition works, references/hover return nothing from the `my foo` call site, but references from A::foo's declaration correctly finds it). Rename appears unaffected (`rename.rs::method_target_with_access` does special-case `inst=="my"` and `override_family`/`workspace_index::method_inheritor_classes` are explicitly mixin/MRO-aware) - checked by source reading only, not executed (harness has no `rename` subcommand).

summary: The assigned note's literal worry -- that a resolver "must walk the class's mixin list, not just its superclass chain" to find `my duplListCheck` (tclopt.tcl:568, mixed in from ::tclopt::DuplChecker at tclopt.tcl:504) -- is REFUTED for go-to-definition and find-references: tcl-lsp already does full MRO/mixin-aware resolution, correctly and unambiguously (verified with an adversarial same-named-decoy class too). But driving hover at that exact call site surfaced a distinct, real bug: `textDocument/hover` returns nothing for ANY `my`/`$obj` method call whose target is reached only via `superclass` or `mixin` (not defined directly on the receiver's own class) -- even though `textDocument/definition` at the identical cursor position resolves it correctly one line of code away in the same request path. Root cause pinned down in rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/hover.rs: `obj_method_hover_text` (~line 2774) does a direct-only `class_def.methods.get(method)` / `class_methods.get(method)` lookup on the receiver's exact class and returns `None` on miss; it never falls back to `analysis.class_hierarchy().method_target(class_q, method)`, the MRO-aware helper that already exists in the very same file (`oo_method_resolution_note`, ~line 2811-2817) and is only ever invoked to append an "inherited from" note *after* the direct lookup has already succeeded, so it never runs when the direct lookup is what's failing.

summary: In `oo::configurable` classes, a class-scoped variable declared inside one class's `initialize {}` block (Tcl 9 TclOO) "leaks" into every other sibling class in the same file that declares a same-named `initialize`-block variable: `classvariable NAME` reads inside a `property ... -set {...}` setter resolve go-to-definition to the FIRST class's declaration in file order (never the enclosing class's own), and find-references merges both classes' declarations into a single 4-location set as if they were one symbol.
failure_scenario:
Assigned note's exact construct (tclopt.tcl:1644-1652, DE class) uses `property strategy -set { classvariable availableStrategies; if {$value in $availableStrategies} ... }` where `availableStrategies` is populated ~300 lines later inside DE's `initialize {}` block (tclopt.tcl:1937-1939). That specific variable name is unique to DE in the file, so the LSP happens to resolve it "correctly" by accident. But the *identical* mechanic one property down in the SAME class (`property initype -set { classvariable availibleInitTypes ... }`, tclopt.tcl:1653-1661, backed by `initialize{}` at tclopt.tcl:1936-1941) uses a class-variable name, `availibleInitTypes`, that a SECOND class (`::tclopt::GSA`, tclopt.tcl:2385) also declares via its own `initialize{}` block at tclopt.tcl:2669-2672. Ground truth (tclsh9.0, minimal repro at .../audit/36/two_classes.tcl, isomorphic to the real pattern with 2 oo::configurable classes each having `property X -set {classvariable V; ...}` + its own `initialize{ variable V; const V {...} }`): the two classes' `V` are fully independent -- `tclsh9.0 two_classes.tcl` prints `Foo correctly rejects Bar's value: Foo: 'red' not in 'alpha beta gamma'` (Foo's -strategy setter rejects Bar's -mode value 'red', proving separate per-class storage; a negative control with the `initialize{}` block removed also shows `classvariable` reading an otherwise-unset variable -> "can't read \"availableStrategies\": no such variable", proving initialize{} is the sole source of the value).
LSP reality (same file, `cd .../audit/36 && python3 lsp_client.py definition two_classes.tcl <L> <C>`, 0-based): Foo's own `$availableStrategies` read at (3,23) correctly returns `13:17-13:36` (Foo's own initialize decl). But Bar's own `$availableStrategies` read at (23,23) ALSO returns `13:17-13:36` (Foo's decl) instead of Bar's own at `33:17-33:36` -- reproduced with class order swapped too (two_classes_swapped.tcl): whichever class is textually first in the file always wins, for BOTH classes' reads.
Confirmed directly on the real corpus file too (copied read-only into .../audit/36/realfile/tclopt.tcl, corpusPath original untouched, md5 83ab6a417c8770599af3deb08691fea2 before/after): `cd .../audit/36/realfile && python3 lsp_client.py definition tclopt.tcl 2421 23` (GSA's own `$availibleInitTypes` read inside GSA's `initype -set` setter) returns `1939:17-1939:35` -- DE's initialize-block declaration -- not GSA's own at `2669:17-2669:35`; same result at GSA's second occurrence (2425,89). `python3 lsp_client.py references tclopt.tcl 2421 23` returns all 4 locations merged: `1939:17-1939:35`, `1940:14-1940:32` (DE's `variable`+`const`) AND `2669:17-2669:35`, `2670:14-2670:32` (GSA's `variable`+`const`) as if DE's and GSA's `availibleInitTypes` were the same symbol -- identical merged set is returned when querying `references` from DE's own usage site (1654,23) too, so it's not direction-dependent. This is a definitive wrong answer on a statically-resolvable case (each class's own `initialize{}` block is trivially determinable as the correct target by walking up to the enclosing `oo::configurable create` body), not an abstention -- and it would make a rename of GSA's `availibleInitTypes` incorrectly also touch DE's unrelated declaration (or vice versa).
Root cause: rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/oo.rs, `Analyser::parse_oo_definition_body` -- the `initialise`/`initialize` member is walked "in the *enclosing* scope (not a method scope)" per the code's own doc comments (lines 294-296, 349-364) and the walk call `self.analyse_body(&body, tok, scope_path)` (line 391-393) passes the SAME `scope_path` for every sibling `oo::configurable create` class at that nesting depth (there is no per-class scope for `initialize`-declared class variables, unlike ordinary instance `variable`s which do get `class_qualified`-keyed treatment via `class_variables`/`var_decl_spans` a few lines above). Two classes' `variable NAME`/`const NAME` statements inside their respective `initialize{}` blocks therefore land in the identical shared `Scope`, colliding on `NAME` and producing the observed first-class-wins definition + merged-declarations references.

root_cause_hint: Three/four parallel `next`/`nextto`-resolution code paths all key off `ClassDef.methods` / `ClassDef.class_methods` (name-keyed maps) and never consult `ClassDef.constructors` (a separate `Vec<MethodDef>`), even though the codebase already has a correctly-implemented analogous function that does walk `.constructors`: (1) `rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/definition.rs::enclosing_method()` (~line 537-549) — iterates only `cd.methods.iter().chain(cd.class_methods.iter())` to find which member's body_span contains the cursor, so a cursor inside a `constructor` body never matches, and `next_dispatch_target()` (line 510-533) short-circuits to `None` via the `enclosing_method(...)?`. (2) `rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/class_hierarchy.rs::ClassHierarchy::next_provider()` (line 126-149) — its per-ancestor filter is `cd.methods.contains_key(method) || cd.class_methods.contains_key(method)`, never `cd.constructors`, so even if a caller correctly identified "class X's constructor" as context it still can't find a provider. Contrast with the same file's `ClassHierarchy::constructor_provider()` (line 101-113), which correctly walks `cd.constructors` for the opposite direction (checking `ClassName new` call arity) — proving the fix pattern already exists next to the bug. (3) `rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/references.rs::method_next_dispatch_spans()` (line 571-589) has the identical `.methods`/`.class_methods`-only lookup, so "find references" to a constructor never surfaces an inheriting subclass's `next` call either. (4) `rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/validity.rs::flush_next_arity_diagnostics()`/`queue_next_arity_candidate()` (~line 1551-1808) feed through the same constructor-blind `next_provider`, so `next`-arity checking is silently dropped for constructors even though `current_method_context()` (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/scope.rs` line 682-702) correctly treats `ScopeKind::Method` as covering "method / constructor / destructor" alike per its own doc comment — the gap is downstream of that, in the provider lookup.

A maximally trivial control with no argparse/oo::configurable at all (control/plain.tcl: `oo::class create ::demo::Base { constructor {n} {...} }` / `oo::class create ::demo::Derived { superclass ::demo::Base; constructor {n} { next $n } }`) shows the same `Definition (0 locations)` at the `next` token (13,8), while the *identical* MRO shape with `next` inside an ordinary `method describe {}` instead of a `constructor` (method_control/m.tcl) correctly returns `Definition (1 locations): m.tcl 5:11-5:19` (the superclass's `method describe` declaration) — proving the gap is specific to the constructor case, not a general next-resolution failure. The note's own specific worry (whether the *dynamic* `{*}$params`-forwarded option subset is ever mis-claimed) is correctly NOT an issue — no diagnostic anywhere asserts specific forwarded option names, i.e. the LSP correctly abstains on that genuinely runtime-dependent part; the confirmed bug is upstream of that, in the basic (fully static, one-level-superclass) "what does this `next` call target" resolution that the codebase's own `symbols`/`constructor_provider` machinery already proves is decidable.
summary: Go-to-definition (and the parallel `next`-arity diagnostic / find-references machinery) for TclOO's `next` unconditionally fails to resolve whenever `next` is called from inside a `constructor` body — exactly the shape `::tclopt::ParameterMpfit`'s constructor uses at tclopt.tcl:500 to forward its argparse-derived, dict-filtered options to `::tclopt::Parameter`'s constructor. The class hierarchy (superclass, constructor locations) is already correctly known to the LSP (visible in its own `symbols` output), but `next`/`nextto` resolution code in definition.rs, class_hierarchy.rs, references.rs, and validity.rs all key off `ClassDef.methods`/`.class_methods` and never consult the separate `ClassDef.constructors` field, unlike the already-correct sibling function `constructor_provider`. Verified on the literal real file at the assigned line, on a faithful minimal repro, and on a maximally trivial control; a same-shape `next` inside an ordinary `method` resolves correctly in all cases, isolating the gap precisely to constructors. A second, independently-verified consequence: a real, deterministic `next`-arity crash into a constructor goes completely undiagnosed while the identical crash shape via a `method` is correctly flagged (E003).

root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/document_links.rs, function `document_links()` (~lines 164-185) together with `literal_file_join()` (~line 220). When the source argument is a bracket expression that `literal_file_join` can't fully reduce to literals (contains `$`, a nested `[...]`, or isn't `file join`), the code falls through to `if let Some(&single) = seg.single_token_word.get(idx) && !single { continue; } path.clone()`. The comment assumes `single_token_word[idx]` is false for "variable substitution / command substitution" arguments, but per rust/tcl-compiler/src/segmenter.rs's own semantics (and its `single_token_tracking`/`multi_token_word` tests), `single_token_word` only distinguishes "one token" from "multiple concatenated tokens" within a word — a whole-word bracket substitution `[file join $dir x.tcl]` or a whole-word bare `$var` is exactly one token, so `single_token_word[idx]` is `true` for these too, and the code wrongly falls through to treating the raw unevaluated text as a literal path, which `resolve_path()`/`file_uri_for_path()` (~lines 273-318) then percent-encode and join onto workspace_root into a syntactically-valid but semantically-bogus `file://` URI. Fix direction: when `literal_file_join` fails on a word whose token kind is a command/variable substitution (or more generally whenever the reconstructed text still contains `$`/`[`), skip (continue) rather than falling through to `path.clone()`; optionally, reuse `tcl_compiler::auto_path_eval::evaluate_auto_path_expr` (already used by `resolve_source_edge` in tcl-lsp-server/src/lib.rs ~11529 for the M9 namespace-rehoming source graph) to actually resolve the common `[file dirname [info script]]`/`[file join ...]` idioms — note that evaluator itself also doesn't substitute a preceding `set dir [...]` assignment for a bare `$dir`, so even reusing it as-is would still require adding simple same-file copy-propagation of a single preceding `set VAR EXPR` to fully solve the note's exact idiom; short of that, correctly abstaining (no link) is the minimum fix. Also worth a follow-up (not part of this verdict): rust/tcl-lsp-server/src/lib.rs's `is_tcl_source()` (~line 12003) extension allowlist (tcl/tk/itcl/tm/irul/irule/iapp/iappimpl/impl/exp/apl) does not include `.test`, so the real corpus's test/test.test (128KB, the actual middle file in this note's chain) would never be picked up by the workspace-folder scan unless explicitly opened in the editor — a separate, likely more impactful gap worth its own finding.

summary: The LSP false-flags "Unknown command" (W123) for any bareword call to a command defined by a package whose pkgIndex.tcl wraps its `package ifneeded` declarations in `if {[package vsatisfies [package provide Tcl] 9.0-]} {...} else {...}` -- exactly the shape of the real georgtree_tclopt pkgIndex.tcl.in (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-tcl-lsp/b4c77bf3-47fd-5ba4-822a-000fa233bcc1/scratchpad/corpora/georgtree_tclopt/pkgIndex.tcl.in lines 5-11), the standard TEA idiom every Tcl C-extension needed after Tcl 9.0 (2024) to pick a Tcl-8-vs-9 shared library. Root cause: PackageResolver::parse_pkg_index in rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/package_resolver.rs (~lines 296-342) only recognises a `package ifneeded` command when it is literally the first words of a TOP-LEVEL command from walk_command_words(content); it never descends into a brace-delimited script body (an if/else arm), unlike its sibling collect_source_targets (~lines 231-256), which explicitly recurses through `[...]`/`{...}`/"..." wrapper words via word_unwrap(). So for an if/else-wrapped pkgIndex.tcl, parse_pkg_index returns an EMPTY Vec -- the package is completely invisible to PackageResolver, even though a byte-identical (modulo the wrapper) flat pkgIndex.tcl, or an if/else-free but equally "computed-string" nested-[list ...] body, both resolve correctly. This starves refine_w123_diagnostics (rust/tcl-lsp-server/src/lib.rs ~11417-11448, driven by refine_workspace_w123 ~11462-11484) of the package's defined-commands set, so it can never rescue the false W123 on a command the package legitimately, staticly-determinably provides. (The W120 refinement, refine_w120_diagnostics ~11304-11333, hits the same blind spot but happens to fail safe there via its conservative "unknowable" branch, so it under- rather than over-flags.) This is a "hard but not undecidable" case: both if/else branches in the real tclopt file (and in my repro) source the exact same Tcl file regardless of which runtime picked which branch, so a human -- or a resolver that recursed into if/else bodies the same way it already recurses into word wrappers -- would trivially get this right.

root_cause_hint:
rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/commands.rs `process_command` (~line 309: `let cmd_name = argv_texts[0].as_str();`) feeds `resolve_command_qualified_name` (rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/scope.rs:363) the round-tripped literal source text of word 0 as produced by `segmenter::word_piece` (rust/tcl-compiler/src/segmenter.rs:166-187), which for a `Var` token re-synthesizes `${name}` from the *variable's name*, never its value — so `cmd_name` is literally the string "${ns}::setdef", dollar-brace intact. `bareword_resolution_candidates`/`command_resolution_candidates` (rust/tcl-syntax/src/naming.rs:691+) then does plain "::"-splitting namespace-candidate generation on that string with no awareness substitution syntax is embedded in it, so no candidate can ever equal a real proc's qualified name and the invocation's `resolved_qualified_name` never matches anything (`indirect` is also hardcoded `false` at every one of these push sites, e.g. commands.rs:364, so nothing downstream is even told the name is unreliable).

This shape is explicitly known and explicitly excluded from the one place that *does* do sound flow-sensitive constant-value resolution: `record_var_or_cmd_command_site` (commands.rs, ~1989-2044) computes `var_name` by truncating the Var token's raw text at its first `}` (so it does see "ns"), but its own comment (commands.rs:2028-2030) says verbatim: "A braced composite head (`${ns}::tail…`) is the W307 ensemble shape... so it is skipped" from `pending_const_dispatches`/`ConstDispatchSite` (guarded by `if var_name == raw` at line 2031, true only for a bare whole-word `$var` head) — i.e. the M7 SSA/constant-value engine in rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/const_dispatch.rs, which is presumably what correctly abstains on the genuinely-dynamic `$cmd`-head findings elsewhere, never even runs on this shape. The W307/W308 diagnostic pipeline (rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/var_command.rs) does record a site for it (`var_command_sites.push`, commands.rs:2041) but that pipeline only emits diagnostics, doesn't feed `resolved_qualified_name`, and mis-models `method_name` as `args.first()` (the *next word*, correct for `$obj method arg` object-dispatch) rather than the literal tail actually baked into the same token after `}` — and even the diagnostic apparently doesn't fire here (0 W307s observed), unlike the already-implemented analogous bracket-substitution case `[cmd]::method` (var_command.rs:994-1017, "FP-OBJ-07"), which explicitly treats a literal `::method` tail as static evidence and suppresses W307. No equivalent literal-tail special-case exists for the `${var}::method` (dollar-brace) shape on either the diagnostic side or the definition/references side.

summary: The note's literal worry (a lexical resolver would misread the nested `proc eHuddleCritcl {bool} {...}` in ehuddle.tcl:413 as declaring a NEW GLOBAL `::eHuddleCritcl` instead of self-redefining `::ticklecharts::eHuddleCritcl`) is REFUTED for hover/go-to-definition: both correctly report `::ticklecharts::activate` in my repro, matching tclsh. But building that repro exposed a real, adjacent bug in the same mechanic: because the analyser's `all_procs` map is keyed only by qualified name and unconditionally overwritten on every `proc` statement (handlers.rs), the SECOND (self-redefining) declaration silently evicts the FIRST declaration's own name_span from the map. `resolve_workspace_symbols` (lib.rs:3989), which both cross-document Find-References and cross-document Rename depend on, tests "is the cursor on a known declaration" via `all_procs.values().find(|p| covers(p.name_span))` — since the outer declaration's span is gone from the map, that test fails for it, the function falls through to an empty result, and `cross_document_references` returns zero cross-file locations. Concretely: "Find All References" from the OUTER (original) proc header returns only 1 location and MISSES both real call sites in another file; the identical query from the NESTED (self-redefinition) header, 5 lines away, correctly returns all 3. A side-by-side control using an ordinary non-redefining proc correctly returns 3/3 from its one declaration, isolating the regression to the two-declarations/same-qualified-name mechanic. Since `rename_proc`/`add_cross_document_rename_edits` route through the exact same two functions, tracing the source shows Renaming from the outer declaration would rewrite only the nested declaration's text locally and emit zero cross-document edits — leaving the outer header's name unchanged and the real call sites in the other file un-renamed (I did not execute rename directly, no CLI subcommand exposes it, but I exercised the identical `resolve_workspace_symbols` call empirically via references). Separately, I found a second, independently-reproduced instance of the same underlying mistake in a different subsystem: the IR/CFG lowering pass (`lower_proc` in lowering/mod.rs) was NOT given the equivalent "nested proc homes to its enclosing proc's *defining* namespace" fix that the analyser pass received — it threads the enclosing *lexical* namespace straight into the recursive body-lowering call instead of switching to `proc_namespace(&qualified)` (a helper that exists and is used correctly elsewhere, e.g. extract_oo_methods_pass). Result: the W214 "unused parameter" diagnostic for the self-redefined proc, and for a plain differently-named nested proc, reports the wrong (global, unqualified) proc name — literally the "misread as a new global proc" failure the note predicted, just in the diagnostics pipeline rather than navigation.

root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-compiler/src/signature_scan/command_prefix.rs, fn extract_prefix_head() (~lines 171-216): only recognises a command-prefix argument that lexes as a single TokenType::Esc (bareword) or TokenType::Str (braced `{...}`, list-parsed via find_element); falls through to None for any other token kind. A `[list procName ...]` argument lexes as a single TokenType::Cmd (command substitution) token, so it is never handled -- the module's own doc comment enumerates exactly "a literal bareword head" and "a braced multi-word prefix" as the two recognised shapes, with no mention of a bracketed `[list ...]` shape, and there is no test anywhere in the repo (grepped for `trace add variable.*\[list` and for `"list"` handling in commands.rs / param_traits.rs / signature_scan) covering it -- this looks like an unhandled case rather than a deliberate scope decision. This feeds analyser::commands::record_command_prefix_invocations (rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/commands.rs, ~line 1229 calling into command_prefix_invocations), which is what populates AnalysisResult.command_invocations for ArgRole::CommandPrefix sites; rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/references.rs::proc_reference_spans (~lines 89-100) filters exactly that vec by head-name match, so an unrecorded invocation is invisible to find-references (and, per its own doc comment, also to document-highlight, code-lens counts, and call-hierarchy). The registry side is correctly configured (rust/tcl-registry/src/commands/tcl/trace.rs: trace_add_command_prefixes correctly flags arg index 3 of `trace add variable ... write` as the command-prefix); the gap is purely in extract_prefix_head's token-shape recognition. A fix would extend extract_prefix_head (or add a sibling path) to special-case a Cmd-token whose inner text is a `list literalHead ...` invocation, taking `literalHead` as the head (mirroring the existing looks_unresolvable guard so a dynamic head like `[list $cb ...]` still correctly abstains).

summary: The mined mechanic itself (ticklecharts::procDefaultValue, utils.tcl:1058-1082: resolves `ticklecharts::$proc` dynamically, greps that OTHER proc's `info body` text for a `-default` token, then does `uplevel 1 [list set $var]` to read a variable whose NAME was discovered by parsing source-as-data) is handled CORRECTLY by the LSP -- it abstains everywhere the mechanic is genuinely dynamic/opaque, and resolves correctly everywhere it is genuinely static. That string is indistinguishable from a genuinely-absolute reference. rust/tcl-syntax/src/naming.rs `command_resolution_candidates` (lines 759-761) then special-cases `cmd_name.starts_with("::")` by returning only the single candidate `::setdef` (global root) instead of trying to recover the true prefix — so `proc_visible_from_namespace`/`resolve_called_proc` (definition.rs:1137,1176) look up a proc literally named `::setdef` at the workspace root and find nothing. The final fallback, `fallback_proc_by_simple_name` (definition.rs:1259), also misses because it compares `proc_def.name == word`, and the real proc's simple name is `"setdef"` (no colons), never equal to the corrupted `"::setdef"`. Fix would need `find_word_span_at_position`/its caller to notice that the character immediately preceding the scan's stop point is `}`/`]` (end of a substitution) and either (a) fold a statically-known variable value (plain literal, or the `self class` + `namespace qualifiers` idiom) into the real qualified name before candidate resolution, or at minimum (b) not treat the residual `::`-prefixed fragment as an absolute name, falling back to a suffix/simple-name match instead.

summary: ticklecharts::gridlayoutHasDataSetObj (layout.tcl:514-533) takes formal param `dts` and does `upvar 1 $dts dataset` -- the classic Tcl call-by-name idiom. It's called as `gridlayoutHasDataSetObj dataset` from ticklecharts::chart's constructor (chart.tcl:28), where `dataset` is never `set` anywhere lexically in the constructor; its only assignment happens via the upvar alias inside the callee (`set dataset [$obj dataset]`, layout.tcl:526), then read at chart.tcl:29 (`set _dataset $dataset`). tclsh9.0/8.6 confirm the mechanism works as designed. The LSP's diagnostics correctly avoid a false "unused/unset variable" warning here (there IS a `ProcArgTrait::VarWrite` + `collect_call_by_name_reads` mechanism in rust/tcl-compiler/src/interprocedural.rs for exactly this). But `hover` and `find-references`, run directly against the real, unmodified chart.tcl at the exact position of the `$dataset` read, both give definitively wrong answers: they resolve the VARIABLE reference `$dataset` to the class's unrelated, coincidentally-same-named accessor METHOD `dataset {}` (chart.tcl:90) -- a `**method**` hover card and a false "reference" pointing at the method's own declaration. This is a clear-cut wrong-kind conflation (Tcl variable and command/method namespaces are always disjoint; `$name` can never denote a method), not a hard-undecidability judgment call. root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-compiler/src/cfg_builder/mod.rs: `detect_upvar_procs(module: &Module)` (~line 1127) builds `upvar_procs: HashMap<String, UpvarInfo>` from a single `Module`'s `procedures` map, inserting each upvar-using proc under exactly two keys: the bare tail (`"setdef"`) and the fully `::`-rooted absolute qualified name (`"::demo::setdef"`) — never the "relative-qualified" spelling (`"demo::setdef"`, no leading `::`) that appears verbatim when a caller writes an explicit namespace-qualified call. `apply_upvar_invalidation` (~line 253; lookups at lines 263 and 283, `self.upvar_procs.get(command.as_str())`) matches the call's `command` text verbatim with no namespace canonicalisation, so that spelling silently misses even within one file. Separately/additionally, `module: &Module` is always a single file's parse — `CompilationUnit::build_for_inner` (rust/tcl-compiler/src/compilation_unit.rs:701-723) takes one `source: &str`, lowers it via `lower_to_ir_with_config`, then calls `cfg_builder::build_cfg(&ir_module, ...)` (which internally calls `prepare_cfg_context`/`detect_upvar_procs` on that same single-file `ir_module`) — so when the aliasing helper is defined in a different file than its caller, `module.procedures` for the caller's file never contains it at all, regardless of spelling. `grep -rn "detect_upvar_procs\|upvar_procs\|prepare_cfg_context" rust/tcl-lsp-server/src rust/tcl-lsp-core/src` returns zero hits, confirming no workspace-wide merge of this fact exists above the single-file `CompilationUnit`. Downstream, `analyser/diagnostics/dataflow.rs::emit_read_before_set_diagnostics` (~line 1004) then sees the call's `defs` list missing the caller-side name and fires W210 on the next read.

root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-compiler/src/signature_scan/command_prefix.rs, fn extract_prefix_head (~line 171-216): only branches on `tok.kind == TokenType::Esc` (bareword, bakes 0) or `tok.kind == TokenType::Str` (single braced/quoted word, list-parsed via find_element); a `TokenType::Cmd` word (a `[...]` command substitution, e.g. `[list procName $a $b]`) matches neither arm and falls through to the final `None`, so the callback head is dropped even though `list`'s own first argument is a literal, statically-known bareword needing no evaluation. Consumed identically by both rust/tcl-compiler/src/signature_scan/walker.rs::record_command_prefix_invocations (background scan) and rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/commands.rs::record_command_prefix_invocations (foreground analyser), so neither ever pushes a `SignatureCommandInvocation` for this call site into `AnalysisResult.command_invocations`. rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/references.rs::proc_reference_spans (shared by textDocument/references and the code-lens reference count per its own doc comment) enumerates strictly over `command_invocations`, so it has nothing to find. rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/definition.rs::definition() (and hover) resolve the word under the cursor by text+scope directly, independent of `command_invocations` -- which is why they already get this exact token right. A fix would teach extract_prefix_head (or a sibling helper) to look through a `Cmd` token whose inner command is literally `list ...` (or `linsert {} end ...`) and treat its first list element the same way the `Str` branch already treats a braced multi-word prefix's first element, when that first element is itself a resolvable bareword.

summary: The namespace-remapping mechanic itself (the note's concern: `namespace eval $ns` where $ns is picked per-iteration by an if/elseif chain, e.g. paths->path, image->img, pixutils suppressed) is handled correctly and is a REFUTED non-issue: this text lives only inside a `puts $fp "..."` string in pixdoc.tcl (never actually executed as real Tcl there), and the LSP correctly creates no phantom namespace symbol for it (`symbols` shows only the 4 real script variables), and correctly resolves go-to-definition/references/hover on the `$ns`/`$name` variables themselves. BUT auditing this exact code shape surfaced a genuine, unrelated CONFIRMED bug in the same lines: the LSP's W220 "dead store" diagnostic falsely reports every `set ns ...` / `set preamble ...` feeding that puts string as "never read", even though tclsh proves the value is read (it's what makes each generated block's namespace name differ), and even though the LSP's OWN hover/references/definition on the same variable correctly find that exact read. Root cause: the SSA dead-store checker's read-detection re-lexes the word's already-dequoted "reconstructed" text from scratch (losing the fact it came from inside a double-quoted string, where braces are inert); an unmatched literal `{` left over in that text (present in pixdoc.tcl's multi-line `"namespace eval ::pix {\n namespace eval $ns {...}\n}"` string, since the outer `{` isn't closed until after the `$ns`) gets misparsed by the fresh re-lex as opening a real brace-quoted Tcl word, which suppresses $-substitution recognition, so `$ns`/`$preamble` never becomes a Var token there and the read silently vanishes from the SSA used-set feeding W220.

root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/dataflow.rs::emit_dead_store_diagnostics (W220, ~L264-408) fires when fu.def_use has no live use for an SSA def. The used-set for a Statement::Call's args is built in rust/tcl-compiler/src/ssa.rs via VarReferenceScanner::scan_word(arg_text, registry) per arg. arg_text is SegmentedCommand::texts's already-dequoted "reconstructed" word text (rust/tcl-compiler/src/segmenter.rs, texts/args()), with the original enclosing `"..."` quotes stripped. VarReferenceScanner::scan_script_uncached (rust/tcl-compiler/src/var_refs.rs ~L168-221) re-lexes that stripped text from scratch via a brand-new Lexer::new(source), as if it were fresh top-level Tcl source rather than "the known-substitutable inside of a string". A literal, legally-unbalanced `{` surviving in the dequoted text (harmless inside the original double-quoted word) is then misparsed by the fresh lexer as opening a genuine brace-quoted Tcl word, which suppresses $-substitution recognition until a matching `}` that never arrives in-scope -- so `$ns`/`$preamble` never surfaces as a TokenType::Var token and silently drops out of the SSA used-set that dataflow.rs consults for W220.

summary: Real pattern (docs/color.ruff:1-4 + docs/utils.ruff:90-197, both sourced by docs/pixdoc.tcl:447-449 with no reference between the two files): file A opens `namespace eval pix::color { variable _ruff_preamble ... }` (relative qualifier); file B independently populates the SAME namespace purely via qualified proc names `proc pix::color::rgba {...}` etc. (also relative, no enclosing `namespace eval`). tclsh proves both land in the one real `::pix::color` namespace. In a faithful minimal analogue (namespace-declared variable in file A, qualified-name procs in file B, no source link needed between them), the LSP correctly merges the PROC side across files (go-to-definition and find-references both resolve perfectly, exact spans) but completely fails to merge the VARIABLE side: hover, go-to-definition, and find-references on the cross-file namespace-qualified variable reference all silently return nothing, even though the identical mechanic works flawlessly when both statements sit in one file. Root cause verified in source: rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/workspace_index.rs's own module doc (lines 19-51) states "Only procs, classes, and command invocations are indexed today ... variables and namespaces are not." Concretely: rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/definition.rs::definition() (~lines 132-143) and rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/references.rs::variable_references() (~lines 286-303) both resolve variables solely via lookup_var_in_scope_chain(&analysis.global_scope, ...) — confined to the CURRENT document's own scope tree — and return empty on a miss with zero cross-document fallback. rust/tcl-lsp-server/src/lib.rs::compute_definition() (~3648-3721) does have a cross-document fallback (cross_document_definition), but it only fires when on_command_head is true (call-site cursors) and, per cross_document_definition's body (~3853+), only ever queries workspace_index's class_definitions_qualified / proc_definitions_qualified — there is no variable table to query. cross_document_references (~4064) mirrors this (test names in lib.rs are all proc/class-flavored, e.g. cross_document_references_finds_sibling_call_sites; none for variables). rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/rename.rs::rename() (~307) also takes only a single AnalysisResult with no WorkspaceIndex, so — by the same architecture, NOT directly tested via the harness (no `rename` CLI subcommand exists) — a rename of a namespace variable from its declaring file would plausibly touch only that file's occurrences, silently leaving a cross-file reference in main.tcl pointing at a now-nonexistent variable. This is a genuine, deterministic miss on a fully statically-resolvable case (no dynamic naming anywhere): the namespace-merge mechanic the finding's note describes is handled correctly for procs but not at all for variables.

The LSP (rust/tcl-lsp-server) correctly and consistently ABSTAINS on the ::pix/::app token used inside `namespace children`: no hover, no go-to-definition, no references, no false diagnostic, no crash -- verified both on the minimal repro (cold, before the generator ever ran, and warm, after tclsh created alpha.gen/beta.gen on disk) and directly on the real corpus file docs/pixdoc.tcl at the actual line/col. summary: tcl-lsp's Find-References (and, by the same shared code path, Rename) never unifies a proc's `global x` alias with a plain top-level `set x`/`set ::x` write/read of the same cell, even though tclsh proves they are the identical variable. In pix's test/data_b64.test, `isEqual {obj b64}` has a de-facto 3rd input: `global tolComp`, defaulted via `if {![info exists tolComp]} {set tolComp 0.01}`, but overridable by any caller that does `set ::tolComp X` at global scope before invoking isEqual (test_fonts.test:249, test_paints.test:34/110 do exactly this). Querying references from inside the proc returns only the 4 in-proc spans and misses the caller's `set`; querying from the caller's `set`/read returns only those 2 spans and misses all 4 in-proc ones. Since Rename (rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/rename.rs:705) calls the identical `linked_var_reference_spans` helper, triggering Rename from either side would rename only half the occurrences, silently decoupling the proc's `global tolComp` from the caller's override — isEqual would then silently fall back to its 0.01 default instead of the caller-intended tolerance, a real runtime-behavior break introduced by a "successful" rename.

root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/definition.rs: `linked_var_reference_spans` (~L886-899) dispatches on `var_def.link_target`; its helper `collect_alias_spans` (~L903-920) unions only variable records whose `link_target == Some(target)`. The root cell's own record (created at the scope actually named by `target`, e.g. by a plain top-level `set`) is never given a `link_target` — only rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/handlers.rs::handle_global_command (~L195-223), handle_variable_command (~L231-269), and handle_namespace_upvar_command (~L2140-2178) call scope.rs::set_var_link_target; handle_set_command (~L154-188) never does. So collect_alias_spans has no way to match "the plain `set` that IS the target" against aliases pointing at it. Same helper is reused by references.rs:311/1284 and rename.rs:705, so Find-References and Rename both inherit the gap. Fix would need collect_alias_spans (or its caller) to also check, for the scope that `target` actually names, whether that scope's own `variables` map has an entry whose qualified name equals `target` (or whose scope-relative name equals target's tail when the containing scope's own qualified prefix matches), and fold in its `definition_span`/`references` even though it has no `link_target` of its own.

summary: docs/pixdoc.tcl:136-140 uses the parallel/lock-step multi-list `foreach` form: `foreach dirName {LIST1} name {LIST2} {BODY}`. The LSP analyser's foreach handler (rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/handlers.rs::handle_foreach_command) only binds the FIRST varList (`dirName`) and silently drops any subsequent varList/list pairs — `name` is never registered as a local variable at all, even though this exact multi-pair form is fully static, unambiguous, standard Tcl (confirmed executable under tclsh9.0 and tclsh8.6) and is even correctly documented/arity-validated in the command's own registry spec. Consequence, proven two ways: (1) in isolation, hover/definition/references/document-symbols on `name`'s uses inside the loop body return nothing at all (pure information loss for a legitimately-scoped variable); (2) directly on the real, unmodified pix corpus file, where `name` also happens to be the loop variable of a later, unrelated, ordinary `foreach name {...}` at line 447 — go-to-definition and find-references on `$name` used inside the FIRST loop's body (lines 143, 152, etc.) confidently resolve to that unrelated statement 300+ lines away instead of the loop's own `name` clause at line 138, a concrete wrong-location bug on the actual corpus file. (Narrower note: the specific sub-question the mined finding's note poses — whether the LSP tracks that `{*}$dirName`'s argument count to `file join` varies per iteration — isn't something any current LSP feature claims; `file join` is correctly variadic so no diagnostic fires either way, so on that narrow point the LSP correctly abstains. The CONFIRMED bug is the more fundamental miss this same code triggers: the second loop-variable of a multi-list foreach is never bound.)
